title: The Clever Thief
summary: A captured thief condemned to the gallows asks for one final boon: to plant a golden pomegranate seed that sprouts only for the innocent.
full_text:
A master burglar named Shafi was captured red-handed inside a royal minister's mansion. Having committed repeated burglaries across Agra, Emperor Akbar sentenced him to be hanged at the city gallows the following morning.

When the executioner asked if he had a final request, the thief replied: 'I possess an ancient family secret that must not die with me. Take me to Emperor Akbar, and I shall gift the crown a treasure of infinite wealth!'

Intrigued, Akbar summoned the thief. Shafi bowed low, held up an ordinary-looking pomegranate seed, and declared:

'Your Majesty, this is a golden seed from the gardens of Solomon. If planted in fertile soil, it will sprout into a magnificent tree within twenty-four hours, bearing fruit of pure solid gold!

'However, it possesses one mystical condition: the person who places the seed into the soil must be completely pure of heart—a man who has never in his life stolen, cheated, lied, or taken what did not belong to him! Since I am a confessed thief, if I plant it, the seed will rot. I offer it to your imperial court so that an innocent man may plant it for the prosperity of Hindustan!'

Akbar was delighted. He turned to his Prime Minister: 'Prime Minister, step forward and plant the golden seed!'

The Prime Minister coughed nervously, adjusted his sash, and stepped back: 'Sire... when I was a youth in school, I once took a gold coin from my father's desk without asking... I fear the seed would rot.'

Akbar turned to the royal treasurer: 'Treasurer, you plant it!'

The treasurer turned pale: 'Alas, Your Majesty... occasionally in my accounts, I have adjusted small expenses to my own benefit... my hands are not pure.'

Akbar looked along the line of courtiers and generals; every single nobleman looked at the floor, made excuses, and stepped backward!

Finally, Akbar thought of planting it himself, but remembered taking a neighboring kingdom's territory during his youth.

The thief looked up at the Emperor with a calm, gentle smile:

'Your Majesty, all these noble ministers, generals, and counselors live in magnificent palaces, enjoy vast estates, and eat from golden plates—yet not one of them is innocent of deceit or greed!

'I am a poor, starving wretch who stole only a handful of bread and silver to feed my dying mother, yet you are about to hang me on the gallows, while these men sit in honor!'

Akbar stood frozen. The sheer brilliance of the thief's trap struck the Emperor to the core.

Akbar smiled with deep admiration: 'Shafi, your wit and truthfulness have saved your life today!'

Akbar canceled the death sentence, granted Shafi an honest post as a night watchman in the imperial gardens, and commended Birbal for teaching the court that true justice must temper punishment with profound humility.
